utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber was informed that you -- that the Defence wished to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I only wanted to provide you with some information about the scheduling for today. In a conversation with the Prosecution, we were informed that they would shorten their cross-examination of the incoming witness somewhat. I informed the Chamber that I would need some more time than the expected, half an hour - about 45 minutes in total - for the incoming witness. And what we wanted to inform you is that our next witness arrived yesterday to his hotel in The Hague around 2230 hours so that my colleague, Mr. Lukic, is working with this witness today, and after the examination of Vojvodic witness today, we probably will not have anyone so that our estimate that we may be working for around two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and thank you for that information, Mr. Stojanovic. I really do not understand why yesterday when everything you're telling us now was known more or less, at least the time scheduled for the witness to arrive was two hours so there was a gap anyhow, and I asked about it yesterday whether there was any problem with whether we would have witnesses or not. No, this week was okay; it was next week that would cause perhaps some problems. Okay. Thank you for the information, but that's exactly the reason perhaps why I inquired into the matter. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another matter is, Mr. Stojanovic, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that next witness should have arrived earlier. I mean, if you look at the time estimates for yesterday and today, you can't just wait. You always should have even a reserve witness ready. Good morning, Mr. Vojvodic. Before you give evidence, you're required to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Could I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated Mr. Vojvodic. Mr. Vojvodic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to say slowly for the record your full first and last name.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Radoje Vojvodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, did you give a statement at one point to the Defence of General Mladic in writing in which you answered the questions that you were asked?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please call up 65 ter 1D01666.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, on one of the screens in front of you you now see this document. Do you recognise the signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the right screen, I see my personal information and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please also show the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, is this your signature on the last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the date, the 14th of August, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, during the proofing, did you have an opportunity to read this statement and point to several points that you noticed than need to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please focus on paragraph 5 on the document we have on the screens in front of us. The document still has the code 1D01666.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, did you indicate to me that in the third sentence, which, at this moment, reads: "I think this was an Egyptian pilot," needs to be corrected so that the sentence would read: "I think that this was a pilot from Ghana whose last name was Evans."

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could now please look at paragraph 12 of this statement. Mr. Vojvodic, did you indicate to me that in this paragraph, in the sentence they suggested that one of them - I think that it was a member of the Spanish contingent whose name was Navaro - the name Navaro should be changed to Romero?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that these two corrections have been made, would you, now that you given the solemn declaration that you will tell the truth in this courtroom, would you fully stand by the statement which you have given in this form with these corrections and does it fully reflect your knowledge about the events that you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. This is my memory, and I would sign this same statement today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would tender the statement of Witness Radoje Vojvodic which is marked as 1D01666.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, I have one question for you. What made you suddenly remember that that person was not Egyptian but from another country and also that you know his name? What happened that what you didn't know a year ago now suddenly came to your mind? Or were you assisted in any way to remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not assisted, but I thought over that, I tried to remember all the members, and his name occurred to me because he was the first one to be released on the 6th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D01666 receives exhibit number D1224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. He was the first to be released on the 6th of June, you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your statement - unless I'm mistaken - I read that they were released on the 18th of June. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had Romero in mind just now. I confused Navaro and Romero, and it seems that there was a misunderstanding between you and me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mixed up ... okay. We'll -- but you at least you now suddenly remembered because he was the first one released but you're mixing him up with someone else; 6th of June; 18th of June. Let's see what happens. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I will now read the summary of the statement of Witness Radoje Vojvodic. Witness Radoje Vojvodic is a biology teacher by education and a reserve officer who was mobilised to the engineer regiment of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps with the breakout of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As of August 1993, he took over the duty at the security organ in the 27th Logistics Base of the VRS Main Staff. In his statement, he talks about what he learned about the possible attack of NATO air force on the building of the logistics base, the removal the weapons and military equipment, and his role in the events which followed after the air force attack on the positions of the VRS. He says that on the 26th of May, 1995 on arriving to the unit at Koran he noticed a member of UNMO, who had been taken prisoner and when he reached the Jahorina Potok facility, he found five or six UNPROFOR members there in front of the depot who were secured by armed persons unknown to him. He was told that these were POWs, as they had sided with the enemy and that there were suspicions that their role was to guide NATO aircraft to the VRS targets. He received a new order directly from the Main Staff of the VRS to accommodate all these POWs in a separate room in his unit's command and to take responsibility for them. He talks about the conditions under which these POWs were allowed to communicate, the visits of the ICRC, the medical services that they were provided, the ability to go outside and their release. He tried in every way to ease their position. He assured them that with a political solution their position would also be solved, and that they would soon be released to home. He let them know that he had no enemies there and that nothing bad must happen to them. He never received any orders in connection with these POWs from General Mladic, nor did he see them on those days. Your Honours, this was the summary of the witness statement of Witness Vojvodic, and with your leave, I would now ask the witness several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the 65 ter summary refers to May 1993 instead of 1995. I take it that this is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a typo, Your Honour. It's not May 1993 but, rather, May 1995. And thank you for indicating this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, could you now please focus your attention on item 5 in the document which is now D1224.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I don't see it in front of me on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see item 5 now?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I see it. Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say, inter alia, that in front of the building you saw "five or six UNPROFOR members who were guarded by armed men who were not members of my unit." Could you tell us how these armed men looked and whether you could at least assume who these persons may have been?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: They wore better uniforms than us. I didn't know them and that was the first time I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The statement further reads: "I asked what was going on and I was answered that they were prisoners of war ..." Could you please tell the Chamber more precisely who did you get this answer from?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: From this group, from those seven or eight people, a tall man stood out. He was probably their commanding officer and he told me that those were UNPROFOR members, prisoners of war, and that, from that moment on, they should be treated as such and then I came up to them. They were tied next to bunkers. I asked them whether they needed anything. Some of them asked for water and I brought it from the guards' room. I brought some toilet paper to one of them. I introduced to them, I told them what my position and rank were and what my name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could now please look at paragraph 6 of your statement. In paragraph 6, you say that you received a new order around 2100 hours to immediately free a building that was used as a gatehouse and put up all these POWs there. Could you please tell us more precisely where, physically, this is located? Where is the gatehouse facility that you talk about in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, this took place in Jahorinski Potok which is around 2 kilometres away from the garrison and the command in the barracks. And I received an order to secure them that evening. Right next to the command there is a building which used to be the gatehouse and it was ordered to get it ready. However, it was only around 21 or 2200 hours that we arrived to the garrison and there was no time then to furnish this room so, therefore, we found a bedroom on the first floor where soldiers used to sleep. It was a dorm room on the floor above the dining room and we put them there. And the next day on the 27th of May around 0900 hours they were moved to the room which was specially furnished for them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, could you please slow down because you're speaking at a speech which our interpreters and transcribers cannot follow. I stopped you when you said: "We put them there and the next day on the 27th of May, around 0900 hours, they were moved to the room which was specially furnished for them." Could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I appreciate. In this room, or the facility, rather, they were from the 27th of May until the 18th of June when they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please, we are both of us too fast. If you can do it more slowly and tell us whether this facility, the barracks, had any name. How did you call it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: During the war, it was called the Milos Obilic barracks. It was the Koran barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did they remain in this facility up until the moment when they were released?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have -- or, rather, look at something, the last sentence in this same paragraph, paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where you say, I quote: "I think I was given this order directly by General Tolimir from the VRS Main Staff." Can you please explain to the Chamber how this system of notification functioned. Who notified you personally about this order that arrived from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: We had a communications department in the garrison and the communications man who worked there told me that they called from the Main Staff and that the order arrived from General Tolimir that I was to take over the security of the POWs, UNPROFOR members who were at that moment in the sector of the Koran garrison. Because Jahorina Potok, where the depots are, fell under the command of the Koran garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did this order that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Sir, I hear you say that the communications -- a man who worked there at the communications told you that there were called from the Main Staff. In your statement, you say: "To the best of my recollection I received a new order at about 2100 hours by radio or telephone." Did you receive instruction by radio or telephone or did you get it from one -- somebody who works -- who told you he had received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember, but I think it was a telephone call when the order was passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which you received. You talked on the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to our communications unit, not to the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you talked to the communications unit, by phone or face to face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not speak to them face to face. I was 3 kilometres away. The message was given to me by telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That clears the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I have a follow-up question in the same paragraph on the last line, sir, you say: "I think I was given this order directly by General Tolimir." What does it mean, "directly by General Tolimir"? Did he talk to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not speak to him directly, but the communications people told me that he, himself, gave the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means that you didn't get the order directly from General Tolimir but through another channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in our communications, we believed that when we received an order, whether by messenger or any other way, it was a direct order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you receive information that General Tolimir was giving this task directly to you personally by mentioning you by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When Mr. Stojanovic read this sentence to you, it was translated as: "Directly by General Tolimir from the Main Staff of the VRS." In the text I read, in the English translation in front of us, I read: "Directly by General Tolimir at the Main Staff of the VRS." Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct that General Tolimir ordered, through communications, that I take over the security duties over the prisoners. I did not speak to him personally but the person from the communications who was tasked with it, got the order to find me and to pass on that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What exactly contained this order? Just to take over the -- the -- your responsibility or any more details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the order was short. To take over responsibility for their security and to place them in a separate room, to provide during the night a separate facility, a dormitory, with bedding and everything necessary so they can sleep there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And all that was part of the order of General Tolimir which was communicated to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a brief order that I executed during the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And nothing further was communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many were these prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the number changed all the time. At the beginning, it was six; then eight; sometimes it went up to 15. First we had only eight beds in these two rooms. I don't know about other sectors in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I only know about the place where I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how did you arrange sleeping arrangements when the numbers increased to 15 and you had only eight beds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some people were moved to other places. There were eight beds beginning with the 27th May in those two rooms, and that number never increased. Only on the day of the hand-over/take-over, there were 15 people because some had arrived from other points, and an exchange was made at the hospital in Korani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying you never had the number 15 sleeping over at the facility that you were supervising?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stojanovic, I would like to ask another question with respect to General Tolimir. Do you know the position he held at the Main Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was in the command of the Main Staff. I think he was chief of security for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everyone knows, it's the Supreme Commander, the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who was that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, I've never been in the Main Staff. I didn't have to know that hierarchy. I was in a lower unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just said: Everyone knows, it's the Supreme Commander, the commander of the Main Staff. Can you tell me the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, in the hierarchy, there was the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, and the commander of the Main Staff was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 11 of your statement. In that statement, you speak about the visits of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and you mention that also in paragraph 9. I should only like to ask you to tell us, to the best of your recollection, while they were at the barracks in Korani, how many times did the ICRC visit.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Twice. Once the visit was to the garrison; and the second time it was at the hospital in the rooms of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these direct visits of the ICRC, did they also contact you through other channels, seeking information about the status of these persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: No, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to the ICRC on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. They called several times and asked about their situation, if there were any problems, if there were any requests, et cetera, and I passed all the messages onto them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did they note after their visits?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: After they visited, they sent us a report in English, and these reports were rather objective and correct. They noted that the psychological and physical state was satisfactory. They had medical reports from competent doctors. They could observe all the time from the air because there was a small park with -- where the guards could spend time, with walking paths, and they could spend time outside. They did not have to stay inside the facility from 8.00 to 10.00 p.m. If the weather permitted, they could spend all that time outdoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many times - bearing in mind what you said in paragraph 12, and you have that in front of you - how many times did doctors come to speak to these persons and check their health?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I personally knew Dr. Mirko Sasic -- Sosic, and Dr. Babic. We had some problems in the beginning, such as with this Romero, the Spaniard, they came and both of them came. Sosic was fluent in English. And on the 26th of May, they stayed there for more than three hours. First of all, making a list, describing the conditions, speaking to every one of them separately, taking their case histories, and suggesting in writing therapy, if any, was needed. Then they also came the next time, made a detailed checkup and a report. And on the 15th of May, Dr. Sosic came with a nurse to take blood and urine samples from Lieutenant-Colonel Njagi, I think the name was, from Kenya. The tests were made at the military hospital and there was nothing alarming about the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Professor Sosic and Dr. Babic was there anyone else on that medical team and what profile of medical personnel?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: There was one woman, Dutch, I think they called her Henny. She was a pharmacist by training and she expressed the wish to supply some supplies, sanitation and toiletries, and she spent several hours talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That report, the doctors' report you mentioned, to whom was it made available?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: To us, to the Main Staff, and it was copied to the ICRC. I remember that woman who was deputy head of mission, Lucy I think her name was, wanted us to give her a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court briefly 65 ter 1D06071. 1D06071. Your Honours, we submitted this document for translation last Friday, but, at this moment, unfortunately, we only have the B/C/S version, and I will make limited use of it. Just to ask the witness, if we look at the last page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I see only the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This document that you see in front of you titled: Report, is that one of the doctor's reports you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the report number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I also want to ask you: To the best of your recollection, on what date was the first visit of the medical team to these members of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: 5 June 1995. I remember that date very well because it was at their suggestion, the proposal of Dr. Sosic and Dr. Babic that we send a recommendation that Captain Romero from the Spanish Battalion be released in view of his depression problems, and our recommendation was acknowledged, and he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you in view of the questions asked by the Trial Chamber. How did that really work? How was he released? And what was your role in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Professor Sosic, who was a regular professor of the medical faculty of the university, he had a lot of authority, as did Dr. Babic. I asked them about this because I feared that something might happen, something that I could not stop or deal with, and they agreed. Everybody received a therapy, but he received a recommendation to be released because he took it all very hard and he had -- he was suffering from deep depression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but how did this process of his release unfold and who took him from the facility physically?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I never left the facility. People from the military police came to pick him up and drove him, I suppose, to the government building. I never left the facility. I never went further than the gate. He said good-bye to all of us. The others gave him a round of applause. Everybody was happy that he was going home after one year's service, but that's all the information I have. After that, we only saw in the news programme in the evening that he had travelled to Belgrade and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how did this process of departure for the rest of the contingent unfold? How did they leave on the 18th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Even before we were informed that the prisoners of war would be released, that morning, we made rounds of their two places of accommodation, the Presidency and the other one, so that they could pick up the remaining items that had been kept in these rooms. They picked up all their belongings and their knapsacks, and all the other members from all the other points joined them. We listed them all. And at the Heliodrom near the military hospital, they were lined up, and I made a short note of record that I was handing them over to Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic. A bit to the side, Professor Koljevic, vice-president of Republika Srpska and president of the committee for foreign relations, was standing there, and Mr. Jovanovic from -- from the Republic of Serbia. I didn't need to go up to them any closer. My mission was accomplished and finished. I shook hands with each and every one of them, wishing them success in their career and to forget, as soon as possible, the moments that they had spent with us that must have been unpleasant. And I believe that the soldiers who were working with me and I personally never were responsible for a single gesture for any move that could have placed them in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to stop you here and ask you to focus on my question. In that period while they were, security-wise, under your responsibility, did UNPROFOR members suffer any threat, any unpleasantness, anything that put them at risk?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: No. There was even one Czech member who received medication or carried medication for a brother who was ill. We took them every day to places where they could have a bath, receive a new change of underwear every day. And at one point they were even unhappy with the quality of the food, although they were receiving the same food as we did. They wanted fruit, and they were given a car to go to the market and buy whatever they wanted and also buy videotapes to watch. I remembered one Brazilian man, Harley, who met some people he knew from Mount Trebevic in the street and they hugged and shook hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06071, Your Honours, I should like to tender this MFI'd temporarily until we receive a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, what number would this document received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D06071 receives exhibit number D1225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Mr. Stojanovic, are you going to provide us with other reports of the doctor as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have them all, but we are waiting for translations. We have another report which is now in the electronic court, but it doesn't have a translation. It's number 1D06072. We can have a look at it even now but only in B/C/S. It's also addressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started with the second report so I wondered what the first report would be to have a bit of a complete picture. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've been able to find English translations of these two reports which we've just now uploaded into e-court so we could have a look at them. I think the translations come from the Karadzic case. 65 ter, if Mr. Stojanovic is interested, is 33087.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, were you aware that these documents were used in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that one of them has been used before, but we had problems with legibility with this document from 1995 because you can see that for yourselves. So we asked the CLSS once again to provide us with an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you see that both reports are available in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, they are there, but perhaps we just have a look at them. Do you want to tender the first report as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, certainly. Also the first report which is 65 ter 1D06072; also to be MFI'd, pending verification and translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy says that it's on our screen, an English translation, so why not be very practical. If there's no dispute about this being the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this being a correct translation then. And perhaps during the break you also look at the other one and see whether the other translation would assist as well. If you wish to tender this one as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you provide a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33087 receives exhibit number D1226, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just can I get some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Moloto would have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is in connection with this exhibit number. Is the 65 ter number 33087 or is it 1D6072? Is it the same document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the one is the number as uploaded by the Defence without a translation and the other one is the complete document, that is uploaded by the Prosecution and carrying -- having English translation with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the Defence 65 ter number relates to the second of the two reports and the Prosecution 65 ter number included both of the 6 June and the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you please be so kind to sort this all out where we have apparently original both B/C/S versions and English translations, to sort out that they are under the right numbers in our system. And then another question, Mr. Jeremy, the second report was marked for identification. Now since you have a translation, would you object against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojanovic, if you'd take care of the right numbering, et cetera, et cetera, then both the reports can be admitted into evidence. Having no further questions, we'll take the break. Witness, we'll resume in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I take the opportunity to briefly deal with P7351, which was admitted on the 28th of April of this year. It is the Zvornik Brigade duty book of June 1995. On the 29th of May of this year, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence through an e-mail that it only wanted to have an excerpt of the duty book admitted. It uploaded the relevant excerpt as 65 ter 18491a, and the Defence has not objected. The Chamber therefore instructs the Registry to replace the current version of P7351 with 65 ter 18491a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies for continuing our business when you entered the courtroom, Mr. Vojvodic. Mr. Vojvodic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find Mr. Jeremy to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Vojvodic. Now, I'd like to start with a few general questions about your position --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to start with a few general questions about your position in 1995. So in your statement, paragraph 2, you indicate that you were assistant for security in the 27th Logistics Base. Now, your formal title was assistant for intelligence and security. That's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And your direct superior was a Major Batinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And your ultimate superior on the professional reporting line was General Tolimir, assistant commander for intelligence and security in the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the 27th Logistics Base where you were based, that was a Main Staff facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: The 27th Logistics Base had its command at Sokolac and we were the first depot in Koran. The 27th Logistics Base --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you continue your answer. You were saying the 27th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: The 27th Logistics Base had several depots; in Sokolac, in Koran, so that -- and the command was at Sokolac, the main command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this 27th Logistics Base was a facility of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on, in paragraph 4 of your statement you discuss the NATO air-strikes on the 25th of May, 1995. In paragraph 5, you say that at this time you were at home on annual leave and you were asked to report for duty, and you were then ordered to go to the Jahorinski Potok facility? That facility was a depot of the 27th Logistics Base; yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify. The first technical depot of Koran had warehouses by the command. And in Jahorinski Potok, there were also warehouses holding ammunition, mines and quartermaster's equipment and it was at a distance of the Koran command of about 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, the Koran facility was a part of the 27th Logistics Base and the Jahorinski Potok facility was a depot belonging to the Koran facility or barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, you have understood well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this Jahorinski Potok depot was a weapons depot; yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I have told you, it was a depot containing weapons and quartermaster's equipment, technical equipment. We had our uniforms there, so that there were clothes and footwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this was -- in Jahorinski Potok location was one of the locations bombed by NATO on the 25th of May, 1995; yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Jahorinski Potok you indicate in your statement that you saw five or six UNPROFOR members outside the facility guarded by armed men who you've already discussed today, and you in your statement go on to indicate that you spoke to these men, that you told them that you would treat them with respect they deserved as prisoners of war; that's paragraph 5. Now, Mr. Vojvodic, in fact, rather than being treated as prisoners of war, certain of these men were told that they would die if NATO bombing continued, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: To clarify, you didn't hear that these men were told that they would die if NATO bombing continued; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Personally I didn't hear it. But later on, in different conditions, they told me that they were placed there as a response to NATO so as to make NATO stop its bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So as a way to deter NATO from bombing the locations that they were placed at; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, NATO had already destroyed several of these depots so I don't know how else one would understand this. I didn't take part in tying them up or bringing them there but we cannot understand it differently than that. It was a sort of military trick or how else to call it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at a video of events on the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could you explain what you meant by "military trick." Is that -- perhaps you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were tied and they were filmed and that was shown on TV. So I think it was more a way of deterring. They believed that NATO would not target its own men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was at the basis of filming them and making that publicly known. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question. You said that they believed that NATO would not target its own men. So it was anticipated that NATO may target those -- those positions where those men were tied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we didn't know what they would target, but they had already destroyed several facilities in the immediate vicinity and it was expected that they would continue to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was just the question -- they just expected they would continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like take a look at a video now. It's P2556. It's already in evidence so I that I we can just play it once and we'll play a short section, starting at 1 minute and 2 seconds and will go to 2 minutes and 23 seconds -- 24 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the booth been provided with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [VOICEOVER]: "It's going to be your life. "You will die for the good of NATO. This is 7-9, over. 7-9 Lima we are instructed to advise you that ... [VOICEOVER]: "They are still shooting up there. Give me your hand. You, there, wait. [VOICEOVER]: "Call. Call Kozirev to save you. Let him fuck you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We stopped at 2 minutes and 23.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see these men chained to posts in front of concrete structures. These men are at the Jahorinski Potok facility; yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I take it you recognise the man that we see on the screen before us as one of the men that you had in your custody?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I cannot recognise him. I can't. It's been 20 years, you know. But all who were in Jahorinski Potok came to where I was later. But this took place before I was informed and before I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I'm a bit confused, perhaps, by paragraph 5 of the statement, what is where. We see here a man tied at a -- whether it's a flag post or anything else, but at least this metal pipe. Now, in your statement, you say you went to the unit command building, and that's where you saw an UNPROFOR member tied to a flag post. And you say you thought it was an Egyptian pilot; you've corrected that. You didn't speak to him. Then you said: "I was immediately ordered to go to the Jahorinski Potok facility ..." Is that elsewhere? The Jahorinski Potok facility. Or is it in the same area as the unit command's building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Jahorina Potok facility is at a distance of around 2 kilometres from the command, and this is a video from Jahorinski Potok. And this is a lamppost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your statement, we find that you spotted an UNPROFOR member tied to a flag post outside the command building. So that's not what we see here, because this is at 2 kilometres distance, Jahorinski Potok, this is where this is filmed. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because in front of the command, as I said, the pilot Evans from Ghana was the one who was tied there. This wasn't that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although that is not entirely clear, but thank you for this explanation. So, as a matter of fact, if we look at this picture at two different positions, people were tied to flag masts or lampposts, whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, in front of the command, and also in Jahorina Potok. These are two separate locations that are at a distance of around 2 kilometres from each other. I hope I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clearer now. You also said that this happened, I think, before you were there, that you wouldn't have seen it. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have understood it correctly. They were all tied already at the moment when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At Jahorinski Potok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also in front of the command. There was a man who was tied there as well. I remember his name and I've mentioned him already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your statement, we read that they were guarded by armed men, not that they were chained to lampposts. Any reason why you did not say anything about this detail which may be relevant for the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stated everything that I remembered. I remember well that Captain Evans was tied. As for the five or six who were in Jahorinski Potok, I said that they were tied also, and quite in detail, but whether they were tied to lampposts or to bunkers is something I couldn't remember. I think that this has refreshed my memory and I believe that this was the location where it happened. I did not intend to conceal anything. It's just that it's been 20 years, and these are details that were not really etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must say that -- you certainly assist me in telling us where you said in your statement that they were tied also in Jahorinski Potok because I had difficulties. But I'm also looking at you, Mr. Stojanovic, I may have missed something but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm following this. In paragraph 5, the statement reads that: "At the command" - and we have clarified now that this was the Koran command - "I found an UNPROFOR member tied to a flag pole and in Jahorina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would you please respond to what I asked. The witness said that he also stated that at Jahorinski Potok people were tied and I was unable to find that and that's what I'm asking you to assist, whether you could find that. It's clear, and I read to him that being tied to a flag post, that's clearly in his statement. But others, all of them being tied, irrespective tied to what, at Jahorinski Potok, I was unable to find, and I was seeking your assistance. Apparently you're unable at this moment. If you find it, then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, when you said you said they were tied there, that's not found in your statement. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, these men at Jahorinski Potok who you've remembered were tied up, these are the men that you refer to in your statement as the men that you approached and told them that they would be treated with the respect that they deserved as prisoners of war for as long as you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said a while ago that I came up to them and that one of them told me he was thirsty. I went away and I came back with a plastic bottle. One of them asked for toilet paper and I provided that too. So I went to each one of them, I introduced myself as I said in my statement, and I stand by that. I never concealed my identity. I told them I was Captain Vojvodic and I told them that I would be in charge of them. But it was normal that I could not make my own decisions. I had to obey my superiors, so I made a tour and I told them that with my honour and my life I would try to make sure that they were safe, that none of the soldiers would come up to them and that at the precise moment when -- and I can't remember exactly when that was, I think it was between 21 and 2200 hours, I received an order that they be taken in a vehicle to the Koran barracks. In the meantime - if you would allow me to clarify - in the meantime, a room where the soldiers slept in the dormitories was made vacant to accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you went well beyond what was asked. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, on the basis of your last answer, if I understand correctly, you're saying that were you able to make your own decisions and were you not to have to follow orders of your superiors, then I do understand you correctly that would you have released these men when you found them chained to these posts?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Look, I'm not a professional soldier, but I don't know whether in any army of the world an officer of the rank of captain could make decisions without asking his superior command about it. The only thing that I could do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that wasn't the question. The question was that if you would have been free to decide for yourself, whether you have released them from their being chained to these posts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not think about that. I don't have an opinion about this. I'm not the sort of person who would resort to the use of force. My task was at the given moment to approach them in a humane manner and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, you've answered my question. One additional question. If chaining prisoners of war to lampposts in the vicinity of what you consider may be a target, in the near future, of bombing, if that would be a violation of the Geneva Conventions, would you still think that you're free not to decide for yourself, and do you think that you still would be -- would you still have to wait for orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I did not take part in tying them up and I was not on leave and there were many armed people around, I did not have such authority to do any such thing. Please don't force me to give you my personal opinion which would be contrary to military rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not forcing you, but if you -- I'm asking you what your personal opinion is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the command, I don't have any personal opinion. Because, in any army, a superior is, rather, the one who is in the right than the subordinate person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would even be true if orders were in violation of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never considered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vojvodic, the man we see on the screen before us is the same man that we saw in the vehicle on the radio repeating or being asked to say that he would die if NATO bombing continued. His name is Captain Rechner. Does that refresh your recollection? A Canadian.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes, Patrick Rechner, a Canadian captain. He fluently spoke Serbian and I communicated most with him. Because he also knew Lieutenant-Colonel Djuricic, who was the liaison officer in the Main Staff in charge of relations. He also knew Vice-President Koljevic who was the president of the committee for relations with foreign countries, and I made it possible for Mr. Patrick to contact the secretary of Professor Koljevic in an attempt for him to get in touch with Professor Koljevic because they were personal acquaintances. I remember that Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I take in your answer that, yes, you do indeed recognise Captain Rechner. Now, he testified in this case that he remained chained to this location for approximately six hours. That's P2554, paragraph 42. Now, sir, you would agree that the treatment that we saw being meted out to Captain Rechner and the fact that he was chained there for six hours, that's -- that treatment is contrary to the Geneva Conventions; yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long Patrick Rechner was tied. Perhaps for another hour after I had arrived. But, in any case, the period was quite long. And certainly instilled fear and -- among them and made them feel uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I arrived around 1930 to the barracks, and then I was at this spot around 2000 hours. And already around 2100 hours, the order was received to evacuate them. If I recollect well, I don't have this noted anywhere but after 2100 hours, they were moved to the Koran garrison, to the room that I explained to you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but the total duration of being tied there, you have no idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir, can we agree being threatened with death if NATO air-strikes continue and being chained at this location is contrary to the Geneva Conventions. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know enough to assess the Geneva Conventions and NATO air-strikes. I would consider it, if it were not related to the air-strikes, I don't know how that fits in with the Geneva Conventions. You insist on me giving you an answer, but I'm not qualified to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask the same question slightly differently. Would you regard it as against the law to tie a person to a flag pole which you anticipate would be bombed? Against the law of the country. Forget about the Geneva Conventions. In other words, you're putting somebody in danger of being killed. Is that not against the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which law governs that. You -- you keep insisting on it, and I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the law of the country where you lived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never heard anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there is any law that governs that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you think it is right your own common sense to do such a thing. Is it correct to put somebody deliberately in the path of danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a different opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] War is, in itself, contrary to common sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about war. I'm asking about tying a person to a pole which you anticipate is going to be bombed by somebody else. Just that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, that day, at least ten bombs fell and there was panic in Pale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: It the correct, is it the right thing to do to tie a person to a pole which you expect is going to be bombed? The simple is answer is yes, it is right, or no, it is not right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you such a brief answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we'll stay on this issue, sir, and I'd like to show you a document related to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 03551 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, on our screens before us is a document dated the same day as the events that we just have been discussing at Jahorinski Potok, the 26th of May, 1995. We see that in the top left corner. And we see that this is a fax from UNPROFOR HQ Zagreb to Annan in New York, and we see a subheading: "Message." And number 1 we read: "Careful consideration is being given to all courses of action available in the present situation. Notes from the commander of UNPROFOR are attached." And, sir, I'll note to you that the -- this commander of UNPROFOR, General Smith, has testified in this case, including in relation to conversations reflected in the note that we'll shortly look at, and that's transcript page 7309 to 7312. Could we go to the next page, please, and we'll take a look at those notes; in particular, number 1. So at the top of the page, sir, we read: "After two air-strikes on the Pale ammo dump, the latter in response to the shelling of the Safe Areas particularly Tuzla, the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at 1730 on 26 May 1995 is outlined as followed: "A. Eight UNMOs are held in Pale, three are handcuffed outside the Pale ammo facility." So the reference is to the Pale ammo facility that's a reference to Jahorinski Potok; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see the report continues and we read: "It is said by Mladic that the remainder are on the roof of the building. He says he is expecting another attack, and the UNMOs will be killed whatever the target." Now, sir, what we read about this report of what Mladic had said that's exactly what these UNMOs who were being held hostage at Jahorinski Potok were told on 26th May 1995, isn't it, that they would die if NATO bombing continued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud. Mr. Mladic, I can hear you. You should take off your earphones so that you can communicate at non-audible volume. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer my question. I'll repeat it for you. What we see as being recorded here, that is to say, that Mladic said that if there's another attack the UNMOs will be killed whatever the target, that's exactly what the men at Jahorinski Potok who were chained to these poles were told on this same date, the 26th of May, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I could not know that. I see this document for the first time. My hierarchy position in the army was such that I had no opportunity to see or hear things like this. You should not overestimate my role and my decision-making abilities in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was, is, whether, what was read to you now, whether that corresponds with what we heard on the video a minute ago. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are putting before me too many documents. I need to concentrate and to think it over. I cannot immediately take a position on something that passes before my eyes so quickly. There are many similarities, but I would need more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, to some extent, the question is asking for opinion so if you'd move on. Of course, the Chamber is able to consider even without witness commenting on it whether there is any correspondence between the two events. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, on the basis of an earlier answer you have provided to me, I understand that you have said that on the 26th of May, 1995, or subsequent to that date, you did discover that these men that we saw chained to these posts were, indeed, threatened to be killed if NATO bombing continued; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I spent a lot of time speaking to them, and that's what they told me. They told me that the people who had tied them up, who had handcuffed them, told them that they would be blown up if there are any air-strikes. But let me tell you one more thing. Our personnel was all around them. They would also be killed. They were no more exposed to the danger of air-strikes than the dozens of soldiers who were with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that was not part of the question. Would you please focus on the question. If there's anything further to be further elicited, then Mr. Stojanovic will do it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And so, when you say your personnel were all around these men, you're talking about VRS personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, the people who handcuffed them who were there. What do I know? I told you at the beginning that I don't know those members of the army. They were not from the units stationed at the garrison, but they were around, some 10, 15 metres from these men. Too much time has passed for me to recollect all the details. And you should really not insist on my personal opinion about things that I was not able to decide about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One short clarifying question. Those members of the army. Which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was army personnel from various units. This unit which carried this out were not our men. They had different uniforms. Maybe there were some para-army, paramilitary. They were all armed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I stop you. You said, "I don't know. Those members of the army." You said, "the army." Which army, again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I was imprecise in my answer. These men were in uniform. They had weapons. I didn't know them. You cannot talk me into admitting that I knew them when I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I told you at the start. Their uniforms were better quality than ours. They had light jackets. I could not really describe it now. It's been too long for me to remember the pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your statement, you say you "saw the UNPROFOR members outside the facility guarded by armed men who were not members of my unit." Did you form the impression that they had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you form the impression that they had a specific task coming from above?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot speculate about things I don't know. What does my assumption mean after 20 years? How can I say whether they had orders from above?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You had orders from General Tolimir. You were in charge of these men. And if there was something which was irregular or unlawful, why didn't you release them and take them inside of the building? You were in charge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have orders to release them then. I was ordered to provide security to prevent anyone from abusing them, mistreating them, provoking them, taunting them. And to provide accommodation quickly. That was the order from General Tolimir that was passed onto me, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is to tie somebody on these masts not abusing or mistreating them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, my task was, in that situation in which these men were at the time, to provide for their security until orders came to place them in the dormitory in the Koran facility. Everything else was beyond my authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to tender that document as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 03551 receives exhibit number P7540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in connection with your testimony about what your orders were and you said that they were -- it was to place these men in the dormitory in the Koran facility, I'd like to show you an order dated the 30th of May, 1995, so four days into the time that you had these men in your custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P5230.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen before us, we see an order from the Main Staff of the VRS -- oh. We did have that. Sorry. Perhaps I misspoke. Could we see P5230. So, sir, very quickly, we see on the screen before us. It's a document from the Main Staff of the VRS, strictly confidential. It's dated the 30th of May, 1995. And if we can go to the last page in each language, please. If we can go one page back, please, in the English. And in the original, sir, we see that it's type signed by Colonel General Ratko Mladic. And if we could go back to the first page, please, in each language, we see the list of addressees, and we see it's to the commands of and included there is the 27th Logistics Base. That was your logistics base, correct, Mr. Vojvodic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the base command was at Sokolac. I never saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained that. So we see that it's an order for preparing, organising, and conducting anti-air-borne assault defence, and if we could go to page 3 -- sorry, page 2 in the English and the B/C/S. In the second paragraph down in the English and the top of the page in the B/C/S we read: "Based on the decision of the Supreme Command, strictly confidential number dated 29 May 1995, in order to take timely measures to prepare for, prevent and effectively counter all possible enemy air attacks, particularly in combatting the helicopter assaults, I hereby order ..." And we see a list of orders. And if we can go to the next page in the English. We can stay on this page in the B/C/S. And focussing on paragraph 7, sir, we read that: "In the course of the day on 30 May 1995, the command of the SRK is to complete the disarming of the captured UNPROFOR members and their deployment to the facilities which have been assessed as possible NATO air-strike targets. The remaining detained UNPROFOR members are to be transported to a safe place; the General Staff VRS, which will organise their transport to other corps is to be informed about their number and location [sic]." So, sir, this intention to use the men held in your custody as a deterrent to air-strikes continued to go on beyond the 26th of May and continued through to the 30th of May, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: No. The men who were with me from 9.00 in the morning on the 27th of May were placed in a room and they stayed there until the 18th of June, apart from that Pole who was released a few days earlier, on the 13th or the 14th, a few days earlier. All the others remained there. And this relates to units that I don't know about. I cannot comment about the PVO infantry brigades or corps. I don't understand why you are showing this document to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, simply if on the 30th of May, 1995 you had received orders to place the men in your custody at targets assessed as potential air-strikes by NATO, that's exactly what would you have done; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Questions conceived in this way ask the witness to speculate what would have happened if something else had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is asked if he would have received such orders whether he would have followed them and that is something that the witness can answer. Please proceed. If you would received an order as written down here, would you have followed that order? Would you have obeyed to that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I told you once before, I don't make forecasts. I did not receive such an order. And I would appreciate it, if you can, and if you will, to discuss more their stay with me on the -- from the 27th May to 18th June and what treatment they received in as far as my competencies are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. What is relevant for us to know is determined by the parties. It's perfectly clear from your statement that you're proud of the way you treated them, by providing them with food, shelter, et cetera. But apparently the parties have different objectives, and they are determining what questions are put, and you are -- you should focus on answering their questions. What you're emphasizing now is clearly in your statement, but apparently there's more the parties would like to explore. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you don't want to answer whether or not you would have carried out this particular order that we see here in paragraph 7 because you know that it's against the Geneva Conventions. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: You keep asking me questions about situations in which I have never been in my life. Things that I have never been at my level of decision making. I was never in a position to decide such things and say yes or no. All I can tell you is that I have no answer to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm moving to a different section now. I think I can probably at the break review my notes and wrap up not too long after the break so it might be appropriate to take the break slightly earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break now. And could you tell us right now how much time after having reviewed. Perhaps it's difficult to say before you review, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I think around 15 minutes, 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you're invited to follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. I have an empty court agenda so I couldn't fill the time with any short matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, we're getting to the end of my questions but I'd like to focus more directly on your specific role in these events. So in your statement, you talk about the mutual trust that you developed with the men in your custody and that you tried to make their position easier every day. That's paragraph 13. Now, sir, as I indicated, some of the men in your custody have testified in this case including Patrick Rechner, the man you recognised earlier. Now, the testimony that he gave in relation to you is that he had many arguments with you about access to the doctors, access to the ICRC and contact with family members. And that's at T18519 in our case, in the Mladic case. Another soldier in your custody, sir, Joseph Galissen, testified that he was so frustrated with you that he actually threatened you with the international Tribunal in The Hague, and that's P397, page 8. Sir, that's actually the reality of the situation that there wasn't this harmonious relationship that you had with your captives, but in fact they were very frustrated with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: No. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: The prisoners of war requested from me something that I was not competent for. Patrick Rechner was a personal friend of Vice-President Koljevic. I know only around 12th or 13th of June contact was established with the office. I think the secretary's name was Ceca and that it was made possible for him to contact him then. He wrote letters to the Main Staff which were forwarded immediately. He wrote a letter to Professor Koljevic which was also forwarded immediately. Not at any single moment did I or the soldiers who were there force them to anything. It was at my insistence that doctors came. I think it is in Professor Sosic's report, "To the request of Captain Vojvodic, I visited." It was on the 5th of June. It was it was at my initiative that a nurse arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: -- for the findings and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... come in on a point that you just made about the doctors. At the start of your answer you said that the prisoners of war requested from you something that you were not competent for and you started now to talk about provision of doctors. Now you also talk about that in your statement where you say, "Naturally during a stay in a facility it was necessary for a medical team to visit and examine their health, although they made no direct complaints.
