" Now, you've testified today and we see in D1226 that the first time doctors came in to visit these men in your custody was the 5th of June, 1992 [sic] so that's 11 days after their captivity began; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the doctors' visit was a result of my assessment rather than their request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you the following. Did you verify whether any of them needed any medication prescribed for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked them, especially two of them, Patrick and Oldrich, were fluent in Serbian, so I communicated with them and I asked them whether they needed anything and all their letters that they wrote, I took seven messages. I remember I sent them to their families --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please focus on my question. Did you verify whether any of those needed any medication that was prescribed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was with them for 15 hours of the 24. Now I couldn't know if they needed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have asked, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could discuss the quality of the food and if we could go to their accommodation and take clean underwear and make it possible for them to wash themselves. I think the medication was not so important. It was in the third or fourth place. I expected them to complain to me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You provided everything to them but you didn't verify any need for medication. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, you've testified that when the doctors did come on the 5th of June, 1995, they identified one detainee who was so ill that they sent him home shortly after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason why I requested the doctors' visit, Professor Mirko Sosic and I had been friends for a number of years, was that Captain Romero could do something against himself because anyone could have seen that he was depressed so I asked them to come. That was number one. And I'm not a doctor to be able to conclude that. It's just that signs of depression were visible on him and to a somewhat lesser degree with the Pole, Kalbarczyk or whatever his name was. I can't remember exactly. And all the others, not at all. They exercised in the park. I remember Captain Oldrich who was doing the pushups - he was a pilot - pushups with his legs wide apart. He would do that there was -- he would do 50 or 100 pushups on this gymnastics apparatus. There was another case, too, the Brazilian Harley, who had problems in his family. May I please finish. Please allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question. You'll have a opportunity to follow up on this area if Mr. Stojanovic would like to after I have finished asking you my questions. Now, you've -- you mentioned a few minutes that you facilitated contact with the families of the detainees and that you took their letters and sent -- and sent those on. Now, Patrick Rechner testified in this case that it wasn't until the 16th day of captivity that any direct contact with next of kin was permitted. And that's the truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: On the telephone, yes. They talked on the satellite telephone. It was limited to several minutes. And Mr. Harley because of the situation, his wife needed to be operated on, he did it five or six days earlier. I can't remember exactly but I received green light from my superiors to drive the Brazilian, Harley, to their accommodation where there was satellite communication so that he could get in touch with his wife. And, in any case, I believe this to have been a humane act. And their families were informed in different ways too, because the secretaries, the interpreters who work there at the accommodation Panorama and Kalovita Brda, the two points I would go there on a daily basis to connect the information. The wife of this Kuldric [phoen] called and Oldrich's sister, Augustina called. I remember her name and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered my question it was that 16 days into captivity that telephone contact was permitted. Now, I'd like to ask about access to the Red Cross which you discuss in your statement. You say that members of the ICRC visited regularly for the duration of their stay in the facility. Now, the first date of the Red Cross visit was on the 8th of June, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Look, I was not authorised to determine when the ICRC would come. They brought a paper from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, the simple question is whether it's true it was on the 30 -- the 8th of June that the ICRC, for the first time, visited those who were kept there. Is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. That was when they brought the approval and then it was fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify something else as well? Would you allow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment just focus on the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if the first visit was on 8 June 1995 and that's 14 days into the period that these men were being held captive, do you consider that regular visitation by the ICRC which is what you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't prevent them from coming nor did I set up their visit. As soon as the approval was issued, the visit took about three or four hours, and no one was present there. None of because was there during their discussion. They made the report and they submitted it to me in the English and in Serbian, and I have no further comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who issued the -- what did you say? The permission to visit the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Koljevic's office. He was the vice-president of the republic and the president of the committee for international relations. It was signed by, I don't know -- and they called me personally from the office to tell me that we should allow this visit to take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And prior to this visit on the 8th of June, 1995, the men in your custody had asked you to see the ICRC on a number of occasions and that request had been turned down until the 8th of June, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: All their requests in writing were written by Patrick Rechner. Each of their requests was addressed to Lieutenant-Colonel Djuricic to the Main Staff and the office of Professor Koljevic and I forwarded them there, and that was where my role ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. That's understood. Now, sir, to finish, I'd like to briefly focus on the release of these detained UN soldiers. Now, this happened on the 18th of June, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And these men were released pursuant to an order from your superior officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: I was informed from the command of the 27th Logistics Base in Sokolac that I should get the POWs ready for release. Then we organised the visits to their accommodation in Panorama and Kalovita Brda so that they could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is not how they were released. The question was whether they were released pursuant to an order from your superior officer. Was there an order by your superior officer to release them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot exactly remember at this moment. Certainly I did receive an order on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that order is received from whom, Mr. Vojvodic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was from Professor Koljevic's office and also the logistics base. Some of the officers there. I received the information that I should make everything ready, make it possible for them to go to their accommodation and collect their personal items which, of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a quick look at Defence exhibit 65 ter 1D06070.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: There isn't a translation for this. We can provide one. I think we can function without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a list of 15 names. It's dated 18 June 1995. Could you -- this is the document pursuant to which the men in your custody were released by you to Colonel Indjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel? Indjic was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. Could you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. The document that we have on the screen before us is the document pursuant to which these 15 men listed here were released from your custody and handed over by you to Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I tender this document as the next Prosecution Exhibit and we'll -- I would suggest it is MFI and we can provide a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, the number under which this document would be MFI'd would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D06070 receives exhibit number P7541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: To finish I'd like to take a quick look at P2560.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Coming up on the screen before us, sir, is a document on -- along the same theme that we're looking at. That is to say, the release of the hostages, the men in your detention. We see that it's dated 17th June 1995. At the bottom of the page in B/C/S we see it is type signed Ratko Mladic. We see that it's addressed to the commanders of a number of different corps in the VRS. The heading is: Freeing of detained UN members. And we read: "In his order, strictly confidential," and a number dated 17 June 1995, "the president of the RS ordered that all UN hostages be released by 1400 hours on the 18th of June 1995." And lower down we see an express order from General Mladic that echoes this order that we see from the president of the RS. And, sir, that's exactly what happened; correct? The soldiers in your detention were released on the 17th of June -- on the 18th of June 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... You're not, but I give you an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... It's because of the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine, but it's common that the one who examines the witnesses so I give ample time. It may even be a matter which I would have raised myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one sentence. My colleague who is a native speaker of English has pointed out to me there is a problem with the translation. The English version reads that the hostages would be handed over, and in the B/C/S version, there is no such word, hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, it's in the first -- yes. If Mr. Ivetic would not have raised the matter, I certainly would have insisted on verification of the accuracy of this translation. Because it seems to be an important -- important phrasing here. Now I even can imagine that whether there's reference to an order strictly confidential by the president of the Republika Srpska, that that order also exists and that it could even be verified whether that's, indeed, the language used in that order. MR. JEREMY, this linguistic issue, could you pay attention that in every respect it is verified, and perhaps even by referring to any original order, that there is no mistake in the use of the word "hostage" in the translation as it appears here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honours, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think that this will take care of the matter. When will we hear from you, Mr. Jeremy? Because I would not only hear from you if there's anything wrong, but the Chamber, under these specific circumstances, would like to also hear from you if everything, having been verified, turns out to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Within the next day or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's say before the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And don't forget to look at what Ms. Stewart puts before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your microphone is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm told that D4 is the original Karadzic order but I'll investigate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's D4, you said. Okay. We'll have a look at the translation of that one then as well. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just, Your Honours, just for the record, let me say that in the B/C/S version of this document, the words are that all detained members of UN be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's argument, Mr. Stojanovic. I asked -- of course, especially in relation to the other language found further down, to verify the language in the reference to the order of the president. But I take it, Mr. Jeremy, that you would include every part of both documents which deals with -- which qualify the persons being released in whatever way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having dealt with that, those were your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were reading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just a final question, Mr. Vojvodic. So in this document, we see the order that detained UN members are freed on the 18th of June, 1995, and that's exactly what happened to the men in your custody; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this order was not addressed to my unit but to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Because in their area, there were other detainees, and I was only responsible for the 15 whom I brought to the specified time -- to the specified place at the specified time as I was ordered on the telephone. And may I add something, please, Your Honours. Would you please allow me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's a direct answer to the question, you may do that; if it's not a direct answer to the question, you're not allowed to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's for you to assess that. I can only say that as for the hostages, I never saw General Ratko Mladic present in Koran and I say that with full moral obligation of the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. First of all, it's in your statement. Therefore, there's no need to repeat it. It's already --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- part of your evidence. And, second, it's not an answer to the question. So would you please refrain from, again, putting your own agenda first rather than to listen to the questions of the parties. And could I have also exactly verified where the witness is interpreted to us as having talked about hostages whether that's an accurate translation. Not that I, in general, have any doubt, but in view of the sensitivity of the issue, I'd like to know whether that's the word the witness used. Please -- no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today on page 50, lines 10 to 12 of the preliminary transcript, you were asked a question about requests for medical assistance. Here is my question: Did you at any point receive requests from UNPROFOR members for medical assistance without you having observed it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojvodic, did you at any point while they were in your charge ever make any threats against these people that their lives would be in danger?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: No. I claim that with full responsibility and all my superiors ordered that no one must mistreat them physically or mentally and they were protected all the time. And during the day they spent most of the time in the park where they walked around because the weather was nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was my last -- to be my last question. You told us that you received such orders from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive such an order from that nothing bad must happen to these people?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: All. Major Batinic, then Djuricic. Major Bukva. I can't remember them all but all the superiors who contacted me, the first question was always that their status had to be decent, humane, that no one threaten them, no one must harm them and accept that we exchanged some army items -- all right. With a soldier in a vehicle they went to the market. They bought things that they were interested in. They went to wash where they were accommodated and to have an exchange of underwear. Not at any single moment were they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... both the market and the washing and the underwear have been mentioned before. There's no need to repeat. We carefully listen to what you say. I would, however, have another question for you. You said you were ordered and you took care that no one would physically or mentally mistreat any of those. Now, do you consider to put those men visibly for the world in close vicinity to what you anticipated would likely be a target for bombing, would you consider that not in any way mistreatment, mental ill-treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I gave my answers only for the period from the 27th May to the 18th of June. During that period, I don't think they were ever mentally or physically at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you allowed them to be outside. You said because the weather was nice. And it also had the result that their presence was visible for the outside world, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, exposing them in that way, to possible harm because you anticipated that the facility might be a target in the near future. Would you not consider that in any way ill-treatment in a mental sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not take part in that, and I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us a minute ago that you -- they were, most of the time, outdoors, and you allowed them to be there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me about the handcuffing before I took charge of them. We didn't understand each other then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm talking about what you testified that there were free to be outdoors when they were in -- when they were spending their many, many days there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I maintain with full responsibility they could spend free time in the park, on the benches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever thought about that being a signal to the outside world that they were still kept in a facility which you considered a likely bombing target in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were no more air-strikes then. I don't know. I wasn't thinking about it. It was just a couple of metres away from the command. My office was 5, 6 metres from them, and 90 per cent of the time I was either with them or in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just one clarification to the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated in response to the President's questions that you gave your answers only for the period from the 27th of May to the 18th of June, which I take to be 1995. Now when we looked at the video footage at Jahorinski Potok of the men chained to those posts and you indicated that you were present later that day, that was on the 26th of May, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE VOJVODIC
utterances.text: Yes. We noted that during my testimony. It was in the afternoon on the 26th May when I took them over and took them to the garrison in Koran where the dormitories were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic. Unless it was triggered by my question, you've had your two rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, but I hadn't completed before you asked that question of the witness, but I would like us to go into private session briefly because I have a question that could follow from the question you asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Nothing else? Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Vojvodic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, either by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing being on the agenda, we adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 9th of September, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of September, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.06 p.m.,
